faqs.question: What is a good Navratri wish to send my boss?
faqs.answer: One or two lines that wish them and their family a happy Navratri and thank them for one specific thing, such as backing a plan this quarter. Keep it to 15 to 30 words and send it on day 1 or the first working morning after it.

faqs.question: Is it okay to wish a client Happy Navratri if I don't know their religion?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the wording assumes nothing. Name the festival, wish them and their team well, leave out any deity, and add a line such as "if you are not celebrating, we hope it is simply a good week".

faqs.question: Should I mention Maa Durga in a work Navratri message?
faqs.answer: Only to a colleague you know observes the festival, and only in a direct message. In a client email or an all-team post, a deity reads as presuming the reader's faith, so a plain "Happy Navratri" is safer.

faqs.question: How do I wish a colleague who is fasting during Navratri?
faqs.answer: Send a short direct message with a practical courtesy, such as moving a lunchtime call, and do not ask about the fast in front of others. Then let them decide; someone keeping a fast may still want the team lunch invitation.

faqs.question: Can I post Navratri wishes on LinkedIn?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the post connects to work, such as thanking the people who organised the office celebration. LinkedIn's Professional Community Policies require professional expression and say the platform is not a dating site, so never use it to ask a colleague to be your garba partner.

faqs.question: When is Dussehra 2026, and does the date change by city?
faqs.answer: Drik Panchang lists Vijayadashami on Tuesday 20 October 2026 for Delhi and Wednesday 21 October for Bengal, and Mysuru's palace calendar also puts its procession on 21 October. Send a Dussehra wish on the recipient's local date.

faqs.question: Should a manager send one Navratri message to the team or one every day?
faqs.answer: One, on day 1 morning in the team channel, plus a short line before Dussehra if a holiday changes schedules. Nine daily posts turn a greeting into channel noise for people who do not celebrate.

faqs.question: Is it okay to send a Navratri GIF or image at work?
faqs.answer: Send one to a work friend on WhatsApp if that is how you already talk. For a boss, a client or a team channel, text is safer, and forwarded images often carry wrong dates, such as Ashtami on 18 October 2026 instead of 19 October.

faqs.question: Is it too late to wish colleagues if I missed the first day?
faqs.answer: No. Any working day of the nine is fine, and Dussehra works as a catch-up for clients. Most people act late anyway: in SubhSandesh's Raksha Bandhan 2026 data, 49.4% of 89 pages were made on the festival day itself.

faqs.question: Can I use the Be My Dandiya Partner page to invite my office team?
faqs.answer: No. It is a one-to-one invitation for a partner, a crush or a best friend as a garba buddy, so it is the wrong tool for a team or a client. Use it only for the one work friend you want to dance with, sent on WhatsApp.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Navratri Wishes for Office: Boss, Team, Clients and Colleagues

The right Navratri wishes for office use are one or two lines that name the festival, wish the person and their family well, and leave out prayers unless you know the reader observes. Match the wording to the recipient: a warm line to your boss, one post in the team channel, a brand-safe email to a client.

Keep it short, and expect to write it late. On SubhSandesh, 49.4% of 89 Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages were made on the festival day itself (a different, one-day festival, used as the nearest analogue, not Navratri data), and 48.3% of all shared pages are opened on a phone.

Below: 20 original wishes for five recipients, a recipient-by-channel table, LinkedIn's own rule, and the 2026 and 2027 dates.

## What makes a Navratri wish right for the office?

A Navratri wish for the office is a festival greeting sent across a working relationship. It works when it is brief, inclusive and pitched the way your team already writes.

Analysing 515 emails from two New Zealand workplaces, [Janet Waldvogel's 2007 study in the Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication](https://academic.oup.com/jcmc/article/12/2/456-477/4583009) found workplace culture explained the use and form of greetings better than relative status, social distance or gender. A stiff formal mail stands out in a "Hi all" team, and a breezy one stands out in a "Dear Sir" team.

## Navratri wishes for office, by recipient

Each group gives when to send, tone, length, then four wishes to copy.

### 1. Your boss or manager

**When:** day 1 (Sun 11 Oct 2026) or the first working morning, Mon 12 Oct. **Tone:** warm, with one specific thank-you rather than praise. **Length:** 15 to 30 words, no image.

- "Happy Navratri, Priya. Thank you for backing the launch plan this quarter. Wishing you and your family a lovely festival week."
- "Wishing you a happy Navratri. I hope the nine nights bring some time away from the screen and plenty of good food."
- "Happy Navratri! Thank you for your patience through the audit. Hope the festival is restful for you and the family."
- "Happy Navratri, and an early happy Dussehra. Thank you for a steady six months."

Skip "best boss ever"; in a reporting line it reads as performance.

### 2. Your team, as a manager

**When:** day 1 morning in the team channel. **Tone:** generous and practical. **Length:** 30 to 60 words, the only message here where a logistics line belongs.

- "Happy Navratri, team. If you are out at garba late this week, mornings are flexible through Friday; just block your calendar."
- "Wishing everyone a happy Navratri. If you are fasting, skip Thursday's lunch meeting, no explanation needed. I will share the notes."
- "Navratri greetings, team. Dussehra is a holiday for our [city] office on [date]; colleagues elsewhere, check your regional list."
- "Happy Navratri! No status updates needed on Ashtami evening. Go dance, eat or sleep, in whatever order you like."

Promise only what HR has cleared. A wish offering flexible mornings is a commitment.

### 3. A client or vendor

**When:** your next scheduled email or a short note on day 1, never inside a dispute thread. **Tone:** brand-safe and secular; name the festival, no deity, assume nothing. **Length:** 20 to 40 words, signed by you rather than "Team X".

- "Dear Mr Shah, warm wishes to you and your team for Navratri and the festive weeks ahead. Thank you for a smooth partnership this year."
- "Festive greetings from all of us at [company]. If you are celebrating Navratri, we hope the week is joyful; if not, we hope it is simply a good one."
- "Happy Navratri and Dussehra to you and your family. Thank you for trusting us with the Q3 rollout."
- "Wishing you a happy festive season. Our office is closed for Dussehra on [date], and [name] will cover anything urgent."

Never attach an offer. A festival wish carrying a discount code is an advertisement.

### 4. A colleague who is fasting

**When:** day 1, or when they mention the fast. **Tone:** low-key, a practical courtesy instead of commentary. **Length:** 15 to 30 words, by direct message.

- "Happy Navratri! I will move our 1 pm call to 11 this week so it is not over lunch, if that helps."
- "Wishing you an easy fast and a joyful Navratri. Tell me if you want the late meeting pushed."
- "Happy Navratri. No pressure to join the team lunch this week; let's do coffee next week instead."
- "Navratri greetings! Hope the nine days go gently. I can take the 6 pm client call on Ashtami."

Offer, then let them choose; someone keeping a fast may still want the lunch invitation.

### 5. A colleague of a different faith, or none

**When:** in a shared channel, as a group wish that singles nobody out. **Tone:** light, with one plain line on what Navratri is. **Length:** 20 to 40 words.

- "Happy Navratri, everyone! For anyone new to it: nine nights of music, dance and goddess worship in many Indian homes, ending with Dussehra."
- "Navratri starts today. If the Ahmedabad team logs in sleepy, blame the garba. Happy festival to everyone celebrating."
- "Happy Navratri to all who celebrate, and a pleasant week to everyone else."
- "Wishing a happy Navratri to those celebrating. Questions about the festival are welcome in this thread."

A private "May Maa Durga bless you" to a non-Hindu colleague presumes a faith they may not share.

## Recipient, channel, tone and length at a glance

This table compares the five recipients by channel, tone and length.

| Recipient | Best channel | Tone | Length |
|---|---|---|---|
| Boss or manager | Direct message or short email | Warm, one specific thank-you | 15–30 words |
| Your team, as a manager | Team Slack or Teams channel, day 1 | Generous, practical | 30–60 words |
| Client or vendor | Email signed by you | Secular, brand-safe | 20–40 words |
| Fasting colleague | Direct message | Low-key, a practical courtesy | 15–30 words |
| Colleague of a different faith | Shared channel only | Light, one explainer line | 20–40 words |

The more formal the relationship, the shorter and more secular the wish. With 48.3% of SubhSandesh's shared pages opened on a phone, 30 words is also a phone-screen ceiling.

## Slack, email or LinkedIn: which channel suits a Navratri wish?

In Slack or Teams, post once on day 1 and let reactions do the rest. Avoid a late-night @channel; 11 pm in Mumbai is 1:30 pm in New York.

Email suits clients and seniors outside your team: the wish goes in the first line, and nobody should reply-all to a 200-person festival mail.

LinkedIn is a public professional publication. Its [Professional Community Policies](https://www.linkedin.com/legal/professional-community-policies) allow "broad conversations about the world of work" but "require professional expression", and bar content attacking people over "religious affiliation". A Navratri post fits when it ties to work, such as thanking the office event's organisers.

The same policy calls LinkedIn "a professional networking platform, not a dating site" and rules out asking for romantic dates there. A garba-partner request to a colleague belongs nowhere near a LinkedIn message.

## When should you send it: day 1, Ashtami or Dussehra?

Navratri 2026 began on Sun 11 Oct, and Durga Ashtami and Maha Navami share one day, Mon 19 Oct, for New Delhi per [Drik Panchang](https://www.drikpanchang.com/navratri/ashwin-shardiya-navratri-dates.html?geoname-id=1261481&year=2026). Drik's default US location shows Ashtami as 18 Oct, which is how that wrong date spreads.

Dussehra is regional. Drik puts Vijayadashami on Tue 20 Oct 2026 for Delhi and on Wed 21 Oct for Bengal, and the Mysuru palace calendar also puts its Dasara procession on 21 Oct. A Kolkata client should get your Dussehra line on the 21st.

In 2027 Navratri starts Thu 30 Sep, with Ashtami on 7 Oct, Navami on 8 Oct and Dussehra on Sat 9 Oct, per Drik for New Delhi.

Our only festival-timing data is Raksha Bandhan 2026: 89 pages, a one-day festival, too small for any per-group rate. Of the 79 pages finished in time, 86.1% came within 24 hours of the day.

So send one wish per person, on day 1 or the first working morning. Save Ashtami for a colleague who observes it, and use Dussehra, on the recipient's local date, to catch up with a client you missed.

## What should you avoid in a work Navratri wish?

A 2026 peer-reviewed CMAJ commentary, [Chaikof, Shah and Najeeb's "Religiously observant faculty, staff, and learners"](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999198), makes two points that apply here. Religious practice is individual, so someone keeping fast days does not necessarily need every other accommodation. And using one member of a group as a stand-in for all of them is tokenism; ask each person what they want.

The authors also advise asking about fasting in advance. For a wish, leave out five things:

- Asking "Are you fasting?" in front of the team.
- Asking the one Hindu colleague to explain Navratri to everyone.
- Naming a deity in a client or vendor email.
- Forwarding an image with the wrong date, such as Ashtami on 18 Oct 2026.
- Attaching a request: "Happy Navratri! Also, can you approve the invoice?"

## Where SubhSandesh fits, and where it does not

The [Be My Dandiya Partner page](https://subhsandesh.in/dandiya-partner) is not a work tool. It is a one-to-one invitation for your love, your crush or a best friend as a garba buddy, so it is wrong for a team, a client or an office garba invite.

It fits one office case: the work friend you want beside you in the circle, invited outside work. The best-friend version asks "Will you be my garba buddy, all nine nights?", carries nine short lines and up to six photos, and ends with a 1080×1920 Dandiya Pass; the recipient needs no app and no account.

Send it on WhatsApp, never Slack or LinkedIn, and only to someone who already counts you as a friend. The interface is English and it does no group invites.

For a colleague's birthday later in the year, [browse every SubhSandesh template](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

## Sources

- Waldvogel, J. (2007). "Greetings and Closings in Workplace Email." *Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication* 12(2). Abstract only.
- Chaikof, M., Shah, P. and Najeeb, U. (16 March 2026). "Religiously observant faculty, staff, and learners." *CMAJ* 198(10). Peer reviewed.
- LinkedIn. Professional Community Policies. Undated; read 12 October 2026.
- Drik Panchang. Navratri 2026–27 and Vijayadashami 2026 dates, New Delhi. Undated.

auditReport.honestAssessment: The only live, substantive incumbent in the US-served top 9 is one HinduTone section of four colleague/client lines; the rest are 404s or homepage redirects, so a recipient-by-channel page with LinkedIn's actual policy text, a peer-reviewed note on individual religious practice and correct regional Dussehra dates has a real gap to fill. The first-party data is thin for this keyword (platform-wide phone share and a Raksha Bandhan timing analogue, no workplace data), and the domain's authority is far below HinduTone's, so expect months, not days.
